newsitem.title: USA: Talbott says new threat could alter NATO pledges.
newsitem.headline: Talbott says new threat could alter NATO pledges.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott said on Tuesday NATO's pledge not to station nuclear arms and "substantial" troops in new member states could be changed if a new threat develops.

He also reaffirmed the U.S. view that alliance membership will remain open to an unlimited number of countries, including Russia, after a first group is chosen in July and he rejected criticism that expansion will dilute NATO's strength.

Talbott's comments, in a speech to the Atlantic Council, is part of a Clinton administration campaign to persuade Americans and the U.S. Senate to back expansion as well as to reassure would-be NATO member countries that do not make the first cut when alliance leaders meet on July 8-9 in Madrid.

In the United States, expansion costs -- $200 million a year for 10 years -- may be debated more than expansion itself and many senators may not support the process if they feel Washington is bearing too much of the burden, he said.

As part of an agreement reached last week in which Russia acceded to NATO expansion plans and settled on criteria for dealing with the alliance in the future, NATO said it had no plans, intentions or need to station nuclear arms on the territories of the new member states.
Aiming to calm Russian fears and opposition to expansion, NATO also stated it would carry out its missions without stationing a substantial number of combat troops in the new member states.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin is to sign the NATO-Russia pact at a meeting with Western leaders in Paris on May 27.
Talbott, in his speech, stressed that "these are...reassertions of NATO's own policy ... They are not negotiated limits on NATO's freedom of action.
"The alliance reserves the unilateral right to reassess the security environment at any time and, if it felt there was a new challenge, to change deployments accordingly," he said.
For its part, Russia said on Tuesday it would reconsider its new partnership with NATO if the Western alliance moved toward offering membership to the Baltic states.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Valery Nesterushkin reiterated remarks by Yeltsin on Monday that Moscow would not tolerate any attempts to grant NATO membership to former Soviet republics.
While not referring to such comments, Talbott stressed: "Madrid is the beginning of a process, not the end. The first (new post-Cold War NATO members) will not be the last."
He said during their summit at Madrid, the NATO leaders will "affirm that the door is open and that no emerging democracy that aspires to full integration is excluded."

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are top contenders to be the first new NATO members since the fall of communism. Romania and Slovenia, if not invited in the first round, are seen as prime candidates for a second wave of new admissions.
The Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia also have been keen to join the alliance.

Despite NATO's commitment to an open-door policy, U.S. officials acknowledge membership for the Baltics and Ukraine would be very problematic, especially in the short-term, because of their geographic proximity to Russia.
Talbott said Russian hardliners have tried to use NATO to "whip up nationalistic passions" and Russian democrats have worried expansion would strengthen those reactionary forces.
"We believe that that risk is both exaggerrated and manageable," he said.

He took issue with critics who argue that any change in NATO, including expansion, would dilute its strength or undermine its identity. "Just the opposite is true. NATO was strong during the Cold War because it was dynamic and faced the security challenges as they existed at the time," he said.
